description:
SPHEREx Sky Viewer

A small web tool for the NASA Space Apps challenge **"Planet X and SPHEREx"**.

Type the coordinates of a patch of sky (or an object name) and watch SPHEREx

images of that patch play like a short video, so moving objects stand out.

## Features

- Search by **RA/Dec** (degrees or `08h55m10.8s` / `-7d14m42s`) or by **object name**

- Plays cutouts **in time order** with play, pause, back, next, scrub bar and speed
summary:
• Purpose: A lightweight web tool created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Planet X and SPHEREx) that turns live NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) image cutouts into time-lapse animations to help users spot moving objects in space.
• Key Features: Supports searching by sky coordinates (RA/Dec) or object name, aligns background stars so moving objects stand out, and offers video playback controls, average-subtraction mode, frame stacking, detector selection (D1–D6), and shareable URLs.
• Setup & Architecture: Built with Python (app.py, fetch.py, processing.py) and an HTML frontend (index.html), it runs locally via a virtual environment and includes a basic non-ML mover detection script (baseline.py) plus offline tests (test_processing.py).
• Current Limitations: Queries can take 30–60 seconds due to live IRSA requests, stacked frames can mix wavelengths (causing brightness shifts), and advanced features like Gaia/WISE catalog overlays or contamination flags are not yet implemented.
details:
The SPHEREx Sky Viewer is a web-based astronomical visualization and transient-detection tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Planet X and SPHEREx). It enables astronomers, students, and citizen scientists to inspect time-series near-infrared imagery from NASA’s SPHEREx mission as an interactive animation to detect moving celestial bodies such as asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs, or potential distant solar system objects.

1. Project Overview & Scientific Goal

• Core Problem: Identifying faint, moving objects (high proper motion or solar system bodies) in large astronomical surveys requires comparing exposures taken at different epochs while keeping background stars stationary.

• Solution: The tool automates querying NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), extracts localized sky cutouts around a target coordinate, performs astrometric alignment, and renders the frames chronologically as a smooth, interactive web video.

• Live Data Integration: Because the application queries IRSA’s metadata tables dynamically rather than relying on a static local database, newly released SPHEREx survey data becomes immediately accessible without code updates.

2. Core Functional Capabilities

• Flexible Coordinate & Name Resolution: Users can search by standard celestial coordinates—Right Ascension and Declination in decimal degrees or sexagesimal format (e.g., 08h55m10.8s / -7d14m42s)—or resolve common astronomical object names.

• Chronological Video Playback: Displays sequential cutouts ordered by observation timestamp with full playback controls, including play, pause, frame-by-frame stepping (back/next), timeline scrubbing, and adjustable playback speed.

• Astrometric Sky Alignment: Reprojects and aligns individual exposures onto a common World Coordinate System (WCS) grid. Background stars remain fixed in place while foreground moving objects visibly shift across frames.

• Reference Target Reticle: Draws a consistent target circle over the queried coordinates in every frame to help track expected positions or verify motion relative to the center.

• Image Processing Modes:

• Average Subtraction Mode: Computes a median or mean stack across the time series and subtracts it from individual frames, suppressing static background stars and galaxies so transient or moving sources stand out.

• Frame Stacking: Co-adds consecutive exposures in groups of 2, 3, 5, or 8 frames to improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for fainter targets.

• Instrument & Field Controls: Allows users to customize the angular field of view (FOV) and filter observations by specific SPHEREx focal plane detectors (D1 through D6).

• Stateful Shareable URLs: Encodes all query parameters—coordinates, cutout size, detector band, and processing mode—directly into the URL (e.g., /?ra=08h55m10.831s&dec=-7d14m42.53s&size=0.05&band=SPHEREx-D2&mode=subtract) for easy collaboration.

• Automated Baseline Detection (baseline.py): Provides a lightweight, rule-based command-line utility that scans aligned image sequences for moving source candidates without requiring machine learning models or GPU hardware.

3. System Architecture & Codebase Breakdown

Component Role & Technical Responsibilities

fetch.py Interfaces with NASA/IPAC IRSA services to query spatial coverage tables for a given RA/Dec and downloads targeted FITS image cutouts following IRSA’s SPHEREx spectral image cutout workflow.

processing.py Handles astronomical image processing: WCS reprojection and alignment, temporal frame stacking, background average subtraction, drawing target coordinate overlays, and exporting processed frames as web-ready PNGs.

app.py Serves as the Python backend web server, handling HTTP routing, URL parameter parsing, orchestrating fetch/processing pipelines, and serving generated frames to the client.

index.html Provides the frontend user interface, search form, detector/mode selectors, and interactive JavaScript frame-player controls.

baseline.py Standalone CLI tool that analyzes processed cutouts using classical image differencing and source extraction to flag potential moving-object candidates.

test_processing.py Offline unit and integration test suite that validates alignment, stacking, and subtraction logic using synthetic test images without requiring an internet connection.

4. Technical Workflow (End-to-End Pipeline)

1. User Query: The user enters coordinates or an object name along with desired FOV, detector (D1–D6), and display mode in index.html or via URL query string.

2. Archive Lookup & Retrieval: app.py invokes fetch.py to query IRSA’s SPHEREx image metadata tables and download matching FITS cutouts. (Initial queries for a new sky region typically take 30–60 seconds due to remote archive latency.)

3. Calibration & Frame Generation: processing.py aligns all cutouts to a shared sky grid, applies optional stacking or average subtraction, renders the target circle, and outputs ordered PNG frames.

4. Interactive Inspection: The frontend loads the image sequence into the browser player, allowing the user to scrub through epochs and visually confirm moving sources.

5. Known Limitations & Future Roadmap

• Network & Archive Latency: Live queries depend on internet connectivity and IRSA server response times, causing a 30–60 second wait on uncached sky regions.

• Spectral Band Mixing: Because SPHEREx is a spectrophotometric survey with continuously varying wavelength channels across detectors, stacking frames across exposures mixes wavelengths, which can cause stationary stars to appear to vary in brightness.

• Heuristic Candidate Detection: Flagged movers from baseline.py are preliminary mathematical hints (subject to cosmic rays or detector artifacts) rather than confirmed discoveries.

• Planned Enhancements: Future iterations can incorporate pixel contamination/quality flags, extracted spectral energy distributions (SEDs), and multi-wavelength catalog cross-matching overlays (such as Gaia and WISE) to distinguish known stars and artifacts from genuine solar system movers.
